name: Manila
info: Manila is the capital of the Philippines, on the eastern shore of Manila Bay on Luzon, where a fortified Tagalog settlement called Maynila existed by 1258 and the Spanish later built a walled city and a Pacific trading port.

facts.founded: A fortified Tagalog polity called Maynila existed on the site by 1258, according to genealogical research; the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi began the walled city of Intramuros on its ruins in 1571.
facts.where: On the eastern shore of Manila Bay on the island of Luzon, in the Philippines, with the Pasig River flowing through the middle of the city.
facts.known: The Tagalog polity of Maynila; the Spanish capital of the East Indies; the Manila–Acapulco galleon trade; Intramuros and Binondo; the British occupation of 1762 to 1764; the Katipunan and the Philippine Revolution; the Battle of Manila of 1945; the People Power Revolution of 1986
facts.today: Manila is the capital of the Philippines and its second most populous city, at the centre of the Metro Manila region.

t: A Tagalog settlement called Maynila stood on the Pasig River by the 13th century and was conquered by Spain in 1571, after which Manila was the capital of the Spanish East Indies for about three centuries.
Its galleon trade with Acapulco linked Asia and the Americas, and its streets held Chinese, Spanish, Mexican, Japanese and many other peoples, with the walled city of Intramuros at the centre.

Britain held the city from 1762 to 1764, the United States took it in 1898, and in 1945 a battle of about a month destroyed most of it before it was rebuilt as the capital of an independent Philippines.
dyk: In 1603 Manila was home to 25,000 Chinese, 14,437 native families and 3,528 mixed Spanish-Filipino families, and a Spanish Jesuit wrote that because so many languages met there the confessional in Manila was the most difficult in the world.
ev: A fortified Tagalog settlement called Maynila is said to exist on the site
Miguel López de Legazpi takes Maynila and begins building Spanish Manila on its ruins
The Chinese warlord Limahong attacks the city and is defeated
An earthquake destroys much of the stone-and-brick city, and another does so in 1677
British forces capture Manila and hold it until 1764
Spain cedes the Philippines to the United States after the Battle of Manila
The Battle of Manila destroys most of the city and civilians are killed in the Manila massacre
The People Power Revolution ends the rule of Ferdinand Marcos

sections.origins:
Manila stands on the eastern shore of Manila Bay on the island of Luzon. The Pasig River flows through the middle of the city and divides it into northern and southern parts, and almost all of the city sits on prehistoric alluvial deposits built by the Pasig and on land reclaimed from the bay. The earliest evidence of human life near the city is the Angono Petroglyphs, dated to around 3000 BCE. Negritos lived across Luzon before Malayo-Polynesians arrived and assimilated them, and the Tagalogs who established the fortified polity of Maynilà were Austronesians. The name is usually read as Maynilà, “where indigo plants are abundant”, or as May nilad, “where nilad plants are abundant”, nilad being a shrub-like tree of mangrove swamps.

The earliest recorded history of the area dates to 900 CE, in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, which shows that a socially complex Tagalog polity, Tondo, existed on the Pasig delta by then. Archaeological evidence shows that the settlement of Namayan, also called Sapa, flourished further up the Pasig in the tenth or eleventh century. By the thirteenth century the city consisted of a fortified settlement and trading quarter near the mouth of the river. According to the genealogical research of Mariano Henson, a settlement existed in the Maynila area by 1258, ruled by Rajah Avirjirkaya, a Majapahit suzerain, until a Bruneian commander named Rajah Ahmad defeated him and made Maynila a Muslim principality. The traditions of its founding range from the mid-1200s to the early 1600s.
sections.growth:
Before the Spanish arrived, Maynila and Tondo were active trade partners of China under the Song and Yuan dynasties and flourished in the middle and later periods of the Ming. Under Spain the city became the colonial entrepôt of the Far East and the western end of the Manila–Acapulco galleon trade, which ran from 1571 until 1815. Silver mined in Mexico and Peru was exchanged for Chinese silk, Indian gems and spices from Indonesia and Malaysia, and crops of the Americas such as chilli, papaya and sweet potato reached Asia by way of the Philippines. After the Ming ban on trade with the Ashikaga shogunate in 1549, Manila became the only place where Japanese and Chinese could openly trade.

A count of 1603 gives 25,000 Chinese, 14,437 native families and 3,528 mixed Spanish-Filipino families in the city, and the walled city of Intramuros and its suburbs held 1,200 Spanish families and a garrison of 400 Spanish soldiers. The University of Santo Tomas was established in 1611. After Mexico became independent in 1821 the Spanish crown governed Manila directly, and banking, industry and education grew more than in the previous two centuries; the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 brought direct trade and communication with Spain, and bridges, roads, railways and ports were extended. Under American rule Daniel Burnham drew up a plan in 1905 for the city south of the Pasig. In 1960 Manila became the first Philippine city to exceed one million people, more than five times its population at the census of 1903.
sections.rulers:
By the mid-16th century Rajah Sulayman and Rajah Matanda ruled the Muslim communities south of the Pasig, which were joined as Maynila, and the Lakandula ruled Tondo to the north. Rajah Matanda was a great-grandson of Sultan Bolkiah of Brunei, and the two cities kept ties with the Bolkiah dynasty and with Sulu and Ternate. Earlier overlords are recorded: Majapahit texts list a territory called Seludong or Selurong, which scholars have identified with Manila, and a Majapahit conquest of the city in 1365 is also reported.

In 1570 Martín de Goiti attacked Maynila for the Spanish governor Miguel López de Legazpi and took it. In 1571 Legazpi returned with 280 Spaniards and 600 native allies, and the defenders set the city on fire and fled. Legazpi founded the Spanish city on its ruins, and Manila became the capital of the Spanish East Indies and of the Philippines, which were administered under the Viceroyalty of New Spain, so that the governor-general in Manila answered to the viceroy in Mexico City. It was decreed the capital of the Philippines in 1595. British forces took the city in October 1762 and held it until 1764, and Spain governed it directly from 1821.

After the Battle of Manila of 1898 Spain ceded the city to the United States, which chartered it in 1901. Japanese forces entered it on 2 January 1942, and American and Philippine troops recaptured it in 1945. In 1948 the seat of government moved to Quezon City, and in 1976 President Marcos made Manila the capital again.
sections.life:
The city was divided by origin and function. Intramuros, the walled city, was built to keep out Chinese pirates and to protect the city from native uprisings, and the Spanish confined the Chinese to a separate district, the Parian de Alcaceria, after the attack of 1574. Binondo, said to be the world’s oldest Chinatown, lay outside the walls, and Ermita took its name from a Mexican hermit who lived there. The Augustinians, Franciscans, Jesuits and Dominicans founded schools and churches, and Manila followed Brunei in converting from Hinduism to Islam by the 16th century, before the Spanish came.

The Spanish missionary Juan de Cobo wrote in the 1600s to his brethren in Mexico that the diversity of the city was immense: Castilians from every province, Portuguese, Italians, Dutch, Greeks, Mexican Indians, African slaves, Javanese, Japanese and Bengalese, and Chinese whose numbers outnumbered everyone else. Burial statistics of the 1860s to 1890s give pure Spaniards as much as 3.3 per cent of the population, pure Chinese 9.9 per cent and mixed Spanish-Filipinos 19 per cent. The city’s growing wealth and education in the 19th century raised a class of ilustrados, whose liberal ideas became the ideological foundations of the Philippine Revolution. Tagalog as spoken in Manila became the basis of Filipino, the lingua franca of the Philippines, while English is the language most used in education and business and Hokkien is spoken by the Chinese-Filipino community.
sections.crises:
Manila was fought over many times. In 1571 the defenders burned the city before the Spanish took it, and in 1574 the Chinese warlord Limahong attacked it with a force of about 3,000 men and 62 warships and was defeated. The Chinese revolted again in 1602, setting fire to Quiapo and Tondo, and in 1662; expulsions followed, though the community usually returned. The earthquakes of 1645 and 1677 destroyed the stone-and-brick city. After the British capture of 1762 the city was pillaged for 40 hours.

In December 1941 American and Filipino forces were ordered to withdraw from the city, which was declared an open city, but Japanese aircraft still bombed it. From 3 February to 3 March 1945 Manila was the site of one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war. General Yamashita ordered the destruction of the bridges and the evacuation of the city, but units of the Japanese navy under Rear Admiral Sanji Iwabuchi refused to leave. Japanese forces killed civilians in what is called the Manila massacre; estimates of the civilians killed range from about 100,000 to 500,000, and women were mass raped in February. Heavy bombardment, American as well, destroyed most of the city, the second most destroyed of the war after Warsaw.

Ferdinand Marcos declared martial law in September 1972, and about 70,000 people eventually became political detainees. After a disputed election in February 1986 a crowd gathered on Epifanio de los Santos Avenue to protect two camps held by defecting officers, and on 26 February Marcos and his family fled the Malacañang Palace.
sections.legacy:
Manila’s galleon trade has been called the first to connect Asia with the Spanish Americas across the Pacific, and the city, with Mexico City and Madrid, has been counted among the world’s original set of global cities. The Philippine Revolution grew in the city: José Rizal’s novel Noli Me Tangere was published in 1886, Andrés Bonifacio founded the Katipunan in Tondo, and Rizal was executed at Bagumbayan on 30 December 1896.

The war destroyed almost all of Manila’s pre-war and Spanish colonial architecture. Some buildings were rebuilt, among them the Old Legislative Building, now the National Museum of Fine Arts, and many historic churches and buildings in Intramuros were damaged beyond repair. San Agustin Church, within Intramuros, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The writer Nick Joaquin described Manila as a city of layers, the Manila of the rajahs, the conquistadors, the viceroys and the Commonwealth, each destroyed and buried before the next rose on the same site.

The Burnham Plan was never completed, and the move of the government to Quezon City in 1948 ended any plan for the government centre at Luneta. Metro Manila was created as a unit in 1975, with four cities and thirteen towns. The city proper had 1,902,590 inhabitants at the census of 2024, and the Pasig River still divides it into northern and southern parts.

summary: Manila, on Manila Bay in the Philippines, was a Tagalog settlement by the 13th century and the Spanish capital of the East Indies from 1571, the western end of the galleon trade to Acapulco. Held by Britain from 1762 to 1764 and by the United States from 1898, it was largely destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt as the capital of the Philippines.
notes: START: no founding date; 1258 is from Henson's genealogical research (the 'by 1258' of the city article), so circa true. The history article places the earliest recorded history at 900 CE (Tondo, Laguna Copperplate Inscription) and says there is no reference to a southern settlement at that time.

DISAGREEMENTS left out or hedged: the date of Bangkusay (city article 24 June 1571, history 3 June 1571) is omitted; the date Legazpi gave the city its title (history: 19 May 1571 or 19 June 1572) omitted; the city article puts Goiti's battle in 1571 and describes Legazpi arriving on 24 June 1571, the history puts Goiti's attack in June 1570 and Legazpi's return in 1571, I followed the history for 1570 and both for 1571; the open-city declaration (city article: MacArthur on 26 December; history: 24 December) is given as December 1941 only; the article calls the British occupation 'twenty months', the history 'two years', I give 1762 to 1764; the Manila massacre toll is given both ways (about 100,000 vs 100,000 to 500,000).

Majapahit 1365: the city article says Majapahit conquered Brunei and Manila in 1365 and named it Selurong; the history article says Seludong is listed in the Nagarakretagama and notes that Potet says no text supports Manila being Seludong. I attribute the conquest to 'one article' and give the identification as scholars'. Brunei/Sultan Bolkiah details are the articles' own and vary (Scott: about 1500).

Islamization: the city article says Manila followed Brunei's conversion by the 16th century; the history article says a dynasty under Rajah Salalila was established in the early 16th century. I wrote only the first, in life, as a conversion of Manila's royal family.
Galleon trade: 1571 to 1815 (history); the city article says more than two centuries. Used the history's years.

Left out as unreliable or garbled: the 'Manila Synod of 1582' and '1599 sovereignty referendums' passage, Latin American soldier numbers, the Cerulean Indult, the Tlaxcalans, the forensic-anthropology ancestry estimates, 'Kingdom of New Castille', the Armenians and France paragraph, the Maharlikas conspiracy, the claim that Manila was only place of Chinese-Japanese trade is kept as stated.

1945: the figures for Filipino troops in the history article (85,000 to 140,000) look garbled and were left out; the 3,000 guerrillas and 35,000 American troops also left out. The city article says the 1945 destruction was by Japanese forces and American shelling and elsewhere by US air force bombardment; I say 'by the Americans as well'.
Population: 1,902,590 is from the 2024 census, written as 'at the census of 2024'. Second-most-destroyed after Warsaw is from the history article (the city article says second-most destroyed).
Section pictures should avoid modern city views.
Martial law: figures (about 70,000 detainees, 11,103 recognised as tortured, 3,257 known extrajudicial killings) are from the city article.
